data.title: A darkroom in a closet, for $180
data.summary: A blackout curtain, a used tank, three thrift-store trays and a fan from the hardware store. How I develop black and white film at home in a coat closet, and what I would buy first if I started again.

thumbnail.alt: A film camera resting on sand at the edge of the water

children.text: Sending film to a lab costs about $15 a roll with scans. I shoot a lot of black and white, so a home setup paid for itself in a season.
What it cost
A used developing tank and two reels: $35.
A changing bag: $25.
Chemicals for about forty rolls: $70.
A blackout curtain and tape: $30.
A clip-on fan: $20.
That is $180, and the closet still holds coats.
Start here
If I started again, I would buy the changing bag first. With it, the only step that needs real darkness happens inside a bag on the kitchen table.

data.title: A type scale for cracked screens
data.summary: Half the phones on a trail crew have a crack across the screen. A small type scale that stays legible through a spiderweb, in full sun, with gloves on.

children.text: We counted: eleven of the twenty phones on our last field test had a cracked screen. The cracks are not going to be fixed, so the type has to work through them.
Fewer sizes, heavier weights
The map uses four sizes and two weights. The smallest label is 13 pixels in semibold; anything smaller vanished behind the cracks in our tests.
Room around every label
Each label gets a halo the color of the map behind it, so a line of the trail never runs through a word. It costs a little drawing time and saves a lot of squinting.

data.title: Designing for people who are offline on purpose
data.summary: Trail crews, rangers and long-distance hikers do not want a better connection. They want software that never asks for one. Notes from two years of building Ridgeline, from the first field test with a trail crew to the sync model we shipped, and what we would change.

thumbnail.alt: A boardwalk trail winding between tall redwood trunks in Muir Woods

children.text: The first time we tested Ridgeline with a trail crew, a sawyer named Dee held her phone up to the sky, waited, and put it back in her pocket. She was not looking for a signal. She was showing me that she had stopped looking years ago.
Most software treats offline as an error state: a gray banner, a spinner, a retry button. For the people we build for, offline is
the normal state
, and a connection is a nice surprise at the trailhead.
Assume the signal drops

We flipped the default. Every screen in Ridgeline renders from what is already on the device, and the network only ever adds to it. No screen waits on a request. If a sync fails, nothing on screen changes; the next one picks up where it left off.
What the network is for
The network does two jobs: it brings in what other crews wrote since the last sync, and it sends out what this crew wrote. Neither job blocks the screen, and neither one is ever shown as a failure.
Cache the next three miles
When a crew opens a trail, we fetch the tiles and reports for the segment they are on and the three miles ahead. It turned out three miles is about a morning of work, and about 6 MB.
The order matters. Tiles first, because a map with stale reports is still useful, and reports without a map are not.
Readable in full sun

Contrast guidelines are written for offices. On a snowfield at noon, 4.5:1 is the floor, not the goal. We pushed every map label past 7:1, dropped the thin weights, and made the "you are here" mark a solid shape instead of a pulsing ring.

content.alt: A small tent half buried in snow at Stevens Pass, under a gray sky
content.caption: Stevens Pass, Washington, 2025. Our test site for glare and cold batteries.

children.text: The best offline feature is the one nobody notices, because nothing ever looked broken.
Dee Halvorsen, trail crew lead
Saying less on screen
Gloves, rain and a pack strap over one shoulder change what a good interface is. We kept to a few rules:
Every action on the main screen is reachable with a thumb, at the bottom.
Nothing important is a swipe or a long press.
A sync status lives in one place, in words: "Saved on this phone" beats an icon.
What we cut

A live crew map, a chat tab and a photo feed all made it into a prototype, and all three came out before the field test. Each one needed a signal to be useful, and each one made the screen busier for the hours when there was none.
What I would do again
Go to the field before writing a line of code. Two days on a trail crew changed more of Ridgeline than a month of interviews. If you are building for people outside,
go outside with them

data.title: Fog on the fence trail
data.summary: A slow morning on Mount Tamalpais, one roll of black and white, and the case for walking the same trail until it surprises you.

thumbnail.alt: A wooden fence running along a grassy ridge trail into the fog

children.text: I have walked the fence trail on Mount Tamalpais six times. On the seventh, the fog came in below the ridge and the fence ran straight into a white wall.
Walk it again
The best photographs I have made came from places I already knew. A new trail asks for attention just to stay on it. A familiar one leaves room to look.
One roll, thirty-six frames, and the fence in nearly all of them.

data.title: My field kit for a week in the North Cascades
data.summary: Two bodies, three lenses, eleven rolls, and the notebook I actually use. Everything weighed, with what I would leave home next time and the one thing I wished I had packed.

thumbnail.alt: A camera body, lenses and film rolls laid out on a wooden floor

children.text: Seven days, sixty-two miles and a lot of switchbacks. Here is everything that went in the camera half of the pack, with its weight.
The list
Two 35mm bodies, one loaded with color and one with black and white: 1.4 lb each.
A 28mm, a 50mm and a 90mm: 1.6 lb together.
Eleven rolls of film in a zip bag: 0.6 lb.
A pocket notebook and a pencil: 2 oz.
Next time
The 90mm came home with four frames on it. It stays home. The thing I wished I had packed was a second lens cloth, after the first one went into a creek on day two.

data.title: Shipping a map app that works above treeline
data.summary: Vector tiles, a 40 MB budget and a battery that has to last four days. What we cut, what we kept, and the one test we run on every release before it goes anywhere near a trail.

thumbnail.alt: Snowy mountains above a still lake under a clear sky

children.text: Ridgeline's map has to fit in 40 MB for a whole ranger district, and the phone it runs on has to last four days on one charge and a small battery pack.
The budget

We split the 40 MB three ways: tiles, fonts and everything else. Tiles got 32. Fonts got 3, which meant two weights of one family and no italics. Everything else, the app included, had to live in the last 5.
What we cut
Hillshading went first. It looked lovely in the office and cost a third of the tile budget. Contour lines every 40 feet replaced it, and crews said they read the terrain better.
The release test
Before every release, one of us carries a test phone on a full-day hike in airplane mode. If the battery is under 60 percent at the trailhead on the way out, the release waits.

data.title: The notebook I keep for every project
data.summary: One pocket notebook per project, numbered pages, and a rule that nothing gets torn out. Why paper is still the first tool I open, and how it ends up in the repository.

children.text: Every project at Switchback Studio gets its own pocket notebook. The pages are numbered, the date goes at the top, and nothing ever gets torn out.
Why paper
A notebook has no tabs and no notifications. When I sketch a screen on paper, I sketch the one screen, not the whole app around it.
Into the repository
At the end of each week I photograph the new pages and add them to the project's repository, in a folder called notes. Two years later, it is the fastest way to answer "why did we do it this way?"

data.title: Two days on a trail crew
data.summary: Before we drew a single screen for Ridgeline, we spent two days with a trail crew in Georgia, carrying tools and taking notes. The first part of a series on building an offline map for the people who keep trails open.

thumbnail.alt: A hiker walking a forest trail beside a moss-covered rock wall

children.text: The brief for Ridgeline was one line long: a trail report tool that works without a signal. We had a dozen ideas for it, and the crew we joined in Georgia threw out most of them by lunch on the first day.
What we learned
Crews write reports at the end of the day, sitting on a log, not on the trail. They want a list of what is left to do, not a feed of what was done. And nobody looks at a phone while holding a saw.
What changed
The report form moved from the map to its own screen, with big fields and no time pressure. The map became the place you look, and the list became the place you write.

data.title: Two nights at Stevens Pass
data.summary: A late storm, a borrowed four-season tent, and a roll of slide film that came back better than I deserved. Notes from a cold weekend that doubled as a battery test.

thumbnail.alt: A small tent half buried in snow under a gray sky

children.text: The forecast said light snow. It meant fourteen inches overnight and a tent that needed digging out twice.
The battery test

I took three phones running Ridgeline in airplane mode, one in a chest pocket, one in the pack lid and one in the tent. The chest pocket phone lost 18 percent over two days. The pack lid phone was dead by Saturday night. Warmth beats everything.
The film
One roll of slide film, metered by hand in flat light. Twenty-eight of thirty-six frames came out, which is better than I deserved.

data.title: What a 35mm prime taught me about interface density
data.summary: One focal length for a whole summer made me stop zooming and start walking. Fixed constraints do the same thing for a dense screen: fewer choices, closer looks, and a layout that earns every inch it keeps.

thumbnail.alt: A silver film camera with a prime lens on a dark table

children.text: In June I put one lens on the camera and left the others at home. By August I had stopped thinking about framing as something the lens does. I walked closer, or I walked away.

Dense screens have the same problem as a zoom lens. When everything can be resized, nothing has to earn its place. The crew view in Ridgeline started with twelve adjustable panels. It shipped with three fixed ones.
Fixed sizes, honest choices
A fixed column width forces the question a zoom never asks: is this worth the space? Most of the time the answer was no, and the panel went to a second screen one tap away.
The result reads faster. People stop scanning for the thing they need, because there are only three places it can be.

data.title: Contour
data.summary: Print-ready topographic posters from any trail.

image.alt: Snow-covered mountains around a deep blue crater lake

children.text: Contour turns any GPX track into a print-ready topographic poster, with your own colors and type. It runs in the browser and exports a PDF at poster size.
It started as a gift for a friend who finished a long trail, and it is open source.

data.title: Darkroom Notes
data.summary: A shot log for film photographers.

image.alt: A silver film camera with a prime lens on a dark table

children.text: Darkroom Notes is a shot log for film photographers: frame, lens, aperture and place, saved without a signal.
When a roll comes back from the lab, the notes line up with the scans, frame by frame.

data.title: Larch Watch
data.summary: A small page that says when the larches turn gold on six North Cascades trails.

children.text: Every fall, hikers ask the same question: have the larches turned yet? Larch Watch answers it for six trails, from trip reports that readers send in.
It is a weekend project that runs for six weeks a year, and then sleeps until the next September.

data.title: Ridgeline
data.summary: Offline maps and trail reports for crews and rangers.

image.alt: Snowy mountains above a still lake under a clear sky

children.text: Ridgeline is an offline map and trail report tool for the crews and rangers who keep trails open. It is used on 1,900 miles of trail in three states.

Every screen renders from what is already on the phone, and the network only ever adds to it. Crews write reports at the end of the day; the next time anyone on the crew gets a signal, everyone's reports sync.
Switchback Studio built Ridgeline for a parks group in Washington and keeps it running.

data.title: I’m Rowan. I make calm software and slow photographs.
data.summary: Designer and developer at Switchback Studio in Bellingham, Washington.

image.alt: Steep green mountains rising around Avalanche Lake

children.text: I’m a designer and developer in Bellingham, Washington. I run Switchback Studio, a two-person practice that builds tools for outdoor brands, parks groups and anyone who works where the signal drops.

Before the studio, I spent four years as a product designer at Cairn Maps, three as a design engineer at Talus Works, and my first job out of school building the online store for Tidewater Outfitters.
What I work on

Most of my work is maps, field tools and the quiet parts of software: sync, settings and the screens nobody notices when they work. I like small teams, short documents and going to the field before writing code.
Away from the desk
Most weekends I’m above treeline with a film camera. I develop black and white at home, in a closet, and send the color film out.
Say hello
The best way to reach me is a reply to the newsletter. I read every one, though it can take me a week to answer.

data.title: What I’m doing now.
data.summary: A short page about what has my attention this month, instead of a busy social feed.

image.alt: A hiker on a forest trail beside a mossy rock wall

children.text: Building
Ridgeline 2.0, with shared crew notes that sync when anyone gets a signal.
A small type scale for maps that stays legible on a cracked phone screen.
Shooting
Six rolls of slide film from a week in the North Cascades, waiting at the lab. Fingers crossed for the larch.
Not doing
Taking new client work until January. The studio is full, and that is a good problem.
